Let it be that even in non-conceptual [cognition] there is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). And thus, by means of cognitions alone, after they have mutually observed one another, the distinction between the agent of convention and the object of convention, as well as the indicator and the indicated, has been established in whatever manner it may be.
We merely repeat such [a view] for the sake of further clarification.

And within that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—brought about by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the experience of ignorance (*avidyā*)—there is a substance (*dravya*), and the genus (*jāti*) and other categories dependent upon it are imagined through the power of ignorance. Furthermore, due to some connection with experience, their natures as shape, limiting conditions, stone, color, taste, and so forth, are distinguished.

Substance (*dravya*) and so forth are non-cognition (*avidyā*) because they are sublated by the non-apprehension of what has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) and so forth possess the status of being objects (*arthatva*) because they are capable of being apprehended; therefore, although substance and so forth may have an object not previously known, they lack validity because they do not constitute [true] objects. As for form and so forth, since they involve the grasping of what has already been grasped, they are of the nature of memory (*smārtatva*). Nor is it a mere fabrication of a dull-witted mind to claim that the subject (*viśeṣya*) and other factors are unestablished.

If this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a transformation (*vivarta*) of substances and so forth manifested through ignorance (*avidyā*), then...
How is it that this [notion] arises in the mental continuum of every living being?
How is it that it has been followed even by great authors of treatises?

And how is it that, despite your own realization that it is ignorance (*avidyā*), you still maintain such an adherence to the conventional usage of "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth? It arises in the continuum of everyone because it is produced by the appearance of determinate specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone is apprehended as substance and so forth, once that is attained—that is, when its purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is secured—the desire is fulfilled; therefore, no sublation (*bādhaka*) is perceived.

The authors of the treatises, desiring happiness, have likewise established this very same principle regarding conceptual cognition:
"In the conventional usage of conceptualization, the fool and the wise man are equal. (Śvarga-kāṅkṣa-vikalpa-vyavahāreṣu samānau bāla-paṇḍitau). [50]

verse 4 (= VP III-3-55).
Regarding knowledge and desire, the fool and the wise man are alike.

The distinction is merely that the wise man has the determination that [the object] is sublated, while the other is a fool. Having observed the moment-by-moment diminution [of afflictions] through the longing for liberation, it was stated that "there is no direct realization of examined objects such as substance and so forth by means of perception."

[51] Śaṅkara says: This is because even for the authors of treatises (*śāstrakāra*), it is possible here to bring together other natures that are not erroneous. For a treatise is undertaken for the purpose of removing delusion (*mohanivartana*). Delusion arises from coarse investigation (*sthūlaparāmarśa*), and that [delusion] departs through subtle, intermediate investigation (*sūkṣmāvāntaraparāmarśa*).

Just as the convention “form” (*rūpa*) is established by virtue of its being the producer of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), so too is the statement applied to taste (*rasa*) and the rest with respect to their own respective sensory cognitions. [56] Therefore, in the case of a jar, a cloth, mud, a sprout, and so forth, “form” and the other [sensory objects] exist by way of a nature that is excluded from what is other than them.
Diverse things are conventionally designated [as one]. The cause of such conventional usage is the cognition of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśapratyaya*).

The meaning is that "reflective awareness" refers to a cognition that superimposes unity upon a single [object of] reflection. Furthermore, that [cognition] superimposes unity by virtue of ignorance (*avidyā*). On the strength of that, people postulate a universal (*sāmānya*);
its negation follows from the fact that no universal form—such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth—is perceived apart from the subsequent reflective awareness of individual instances.

"Like a flower in the sky.

Even though there is difference, certain things are restricted by their own nature in accomplishing a single purpose—such as a unified reflective awareness, an object, or a cognition—just like the sense faculties and so forth. [63]

The distinction between that and what is not that also occurs simultaneously through the predominance of a single synthetic awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*). Consequently, one need not resort to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*).

For this very reason, there is no contradiction in the engagement with linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), because the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized object (*vikalpya*) are unified; the perceived object is grasped as something vividly manifest.

If it is argued that [determination] is not otherwise than as "this-ness" (*idantā*), [we reply: knowledge qualified by "this-ness" is neither perception—since perception consists in the ascertainment of a proximate object and depends upon the sense organs—nor does it depend on both [the object and the senses], because it is independent of both. This is merely the conceit of direct perception on the part of bad logicians, since direct perception does not apply here.
[178] Because it is not present as a direct perception.
[178] This is a case of *māna* (pride); [in the plural], it is *māna* in these [objects].

And it has been said [Sh42]: “The error consisting of the mental recollection following upon seeing and touching is purely mental. Because the conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) of a substance—based on the thought, “I am touching that very same thing which I saw”—is established solely through delusion (*bhrānti*). Therefore, the sense organ does not perceive the object as qualified by a specific mental construction.
[179] There is no positive concomitance with the observation.
[181] That very thing is marked by the Great Seal (mahāmudrā); it is indeed that which is characterized by the Great Seal.
[182] NBh ad NS 3, 1, 1: “… that which I saw with the eye, that I touch with the sense of touch…”; NV ad NS 1, 1, 14: “… that which I saw, that I touch…”.
[183] From the Śābarabhāṣya (Sh). Because of the lack of logical connection (al-pāt).

That which exists both in each individual [atom] and in the aggregate is the nature (*rūpa*) of the entity, such as blueness (*nīlatva*). That which does not exist in each individual but exists in the aggregate is a property of the aggregate (*samudāyadharma*), such as squareness (*caturasratva*) and so forth. However, grossness (*sthūlya*) is a property that appears in the aggregate. When many [atoms] appear without interval, there arises the cognition "gross. Therefore, by this—
Visible form or touch is gross, but there is no substance over and above them that is gross, because such a thing does not appear.
[184] Cf. TR 43,7–8: “For white color exists both in each individual [atom] and in the aggregate; this is the form of the real entity.”

DhPr 42, 23–24 (“The configuration (*sanniveśa*)—such as being quadrangular and so forth—is a property of appearance (*pratibhāsa-dharma*”) ; 43, 9–10 (“This single gross [object] is called a property of appearance because it is established on the basis of such an appearance. It is not a property of the real entity (*vastu-dharma*), for [the parts] individually...”)

PVinT 10b2-3: "When many [atoms] appear to a single cognition, their being situated in a location that is an aggregate of shapes such as 'long' and so forth is a property of the individual appearances (*pratyeka-pratibhāsa*), but it is not a property of the [external] entity (*vastu*).
Therefore, if whiteness is not apprehended, neither its own property nor the shape of another's property is apprehended."
Because it is deceptive, the cognition of [something] as yellow is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[186] M-pratibhāsa. [187] Cf. TBh 66, 18–19: “If this is so, how is it that Dharmottara stated that ‘grossness is a property of the appearance’ (*pratibhāsa-dharma*)?”

Now, if grossness is a property of appearance, then is it internal or external? If you say that it is not internal and not external, but rather something non-existent that has been superimposed, then it must be stated that it simply does not exist at all. Why, then, is it said that "grossness is a property of appearance"? True.
Coarseness (*sthaulya*) is a form that has turned away from the non-coarse;

it is not some positive entity. Therefore, although it is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), it is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*) because it is treated as such through the conceptualization of the coarse;
yet it is not non-existent in every respect. It exists exactly as a universal (*sāmānya*) by virtue of being the object of a single unifying reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*). And it is said:
[189] M & Sh *niḥsvabhāvatvam*. [190] M & Sh *niḥsvabhāvatvam*.
[191] Śālikanātha:

"Because it is the cause of a coarse reflective awareness, cognition possesses coarseness; by virtue of being the cause of a coarse cognition, the coarseness of entities is likewise maintained. [192–193]

[192] M repeats *venabhā*. [193] Cf. PV I 109: “Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), cognition is non-differentiating; by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition, even individual manifestations (*vyakti*) possess non-difference.”
If it is asked, "Does the very act of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) itself superimpose the gross?
[the reply is: "There is indeed such a thing as that which arises from an internal disturbance; by its very nature, arising from a defect, it presents a false appearance. [194]

By this reasoning, it has been stated more than once that [the error] arises because it is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the experience of ignorance (*avidyā*). [195][196] Therefore, even though there is the appearance of "a coarse blue," there is no delusion regarding the blue thing-in-itself (*vasturūpa*). The delusion, however, is the appearance of yellow in a conch shell.
For white color exists both individually and in a collection as the form (*rūpa*) of a real entity (*vastu*); and shape (*saṃsthāna*) is a property (*dharma*) of that collection.
[197] Sh ta.
[198] M: In the case of *śukla*.
[199] Ś: In the case of a collection (*samudaya*). [200] Cf. TR 42, 5: “That which exists both in each individual and in the collection is the nature of the entity.”

When there is no appearance of white, there is likewise no appearance of the aggregate that constitutes its nature. Consequently, the cognition of a yellow conch-shell is not corroborated even in part, nor does it directly perceive the actual object. Therefore, the two qualifiers are included for the purpose of refuting misconceptions.
Furthermore, regarding erroneous cognition [201]:

“Because it is supramundane, because of the conjunction with both natures, because of the loss of memory, and because of distorted cognitions,” and so forth—such are the various conventional designations. Regarding these, we do not dispute over the names. However, the ultimate truth is that the nature of the intended object has not been directly realized.
[201] M again: bhrā-... [202]
[202] M-citter:
“Therefore, cognition arising from that object is perception”—this definition by the venerable teacher Vasubandhu is deficient.
The Naiyāyika definition is: “Cognition produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature.”

"Perception (*pratyakṣa*). According to the Vaiśeṣikas: "Among substances, that perception which arises from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object is distinct [from inference]. [Sh44] For the followers of Kapila as well: "The functioning of the ear and other senses is perception. The functioning of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, presided over by the mind, operating respectively in the apprehension of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception."

In the *Mīmāṃsā* [Sūtra], it is stated: "When there is contact of a person's sense organs with what is existent, the arising of cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*). All of this is incorrect because it refutes [the existence of] substance, quality, self, and so forth.
[205] *Śom.* omits *ātma*.
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Determination of the Logic of the Definitions of Direct Perception for Oneself and Others," in the *Tarkarahasya*.
